name: xquad
description: A hardware-agnostic SDK for optimization problems: define a problem once, then lower it to any quantum or classical solver
readmeExcerpt:
# XQuad

> **Early public release.** The instruction set, binary format, and public API
> may still change before v1.0. Production use is not recommended yet.

XQuad is a hardware-agnostic toolchain for expressing and running quadratic
optimization problems (QUBO / Ising / integer) across quantum annealers and
classical solvers. It ships as two Rust crates plus five Python distributions
built around a single virtual-machine specification.

Think of it as **LLVM for quadratic models** -- a common intermediate
representation that lets you write a problem once and retarget it to any
supported backend.

- **Spec-first.** Every behaviour is nailed down in [`spec/xqvm/SPEC.md`](spec/xqvm/SPEC.md)
  and cross-implementation parity is mechanically enforced: every committed
  conformance vector runs on both the Rust production VM (`xqvm`) and the
  Python reference VM (`xqvm_py`) in CI; disagreement fails the build.
- **Embeddable.** The Rust core supports `no_std + alloc`, so the same VM
  runs inside WASM runtimes, Substrate pallets, and native binaries.
- **Interactive.** The Python umbrella (`xquad`) is REPL and Jupyter-friendly:
  load a program once, run it with different calldata, inspect outputs by
  slot. Low-level FFI lives in `xqffi`; user-facing `Program` / `Session` /
  `RunResult` live in `xquad.program`.

## Install

### Python (from PyPI)

Install XQuad into a project environment first: a virtual environment, or a `uv` project.

```sh
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install xquad
# or, in a uv project:
uv add xquad
```

For the `xquad` command alone, outside any project, install it as a `uv` tool, with the `quip` extra for the `xquad quip` commands:

```sh
uv tool install xquad            # the xquad command
uv tool install 'xquad[quip]'    # with the xquad quip commands
```

On macOS, a user install (`pip install --user`, or pip falling back to one) puts the `xquad` command in `~/Library/Python/3.x/bin`, which is not on `PATH`; `python -m xquad` runs the same command without it.

The `xquad` package is the umbrella: the full pipeline and the `xquad` command. To pick individual pieces instead, install `xqffi`, `xqcp` and `xqsa` (FFI bindings, DSL, solvers). Prebuilt wheels are available for Linux x86_64 and aarch64 (CPython >= 3.13). On macOS and Windows, pip builds the `xqffi` Rust extension from source -- this requires a [Rust toolchain](https://rustup.rs/) (>= 1.85).

### GPU/QPU support

The base install includes CPU simulated annealing only. To use GPU or quantum hardware solvers, install the corresponding extra:

| Solver | Install | Prerequisite |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| NVIDIA CUDA GPU (`cuda-gpu`) | `pip install 'xquad[cuda]'` | CUDA 12.x driver + NVIDIA GPU |
| Apple Metal GPU (`metal-gpu`) | `pip install 'xquad[metal]'` | Apple Silicon Mac with a Metal device |
| D-Wave Advantage QPU (`dwave-qpu`) | `pip install 'xquad[dwave]'` | D-Wave Leap account + API token |
| Quip Network solver (`quip`) | `pip install 'xquad[quip]'` | `QUIP_RPC_URL` + a configured signer |

Extras are composable: `pip install 'xquad[cuda,dwave]'`. See [`xqsa/README.md`](xqsa/README.md#install) for driver prerequisites and per-solver quick-starts.

For a guided walkthrough that installs XQuad, verifies it, and runs a
complete problem end to end, see
[Install XQuad](docs/book/src/start/README.md) in the book.

## Package map

Two Rust crates on **crates.io**:

| Crate | Description |
|---|---|
| [`xqvm`](xqvm/) | X-Quadratic Virtual Machine interpreter, bytecode codec, opcode table (`no_std + alloc`) |
| [`xqasm`](xqasm/) | `.xqasm` text-format assembler |

Five Python distributions on **PyPI**:

| Package | Description |
|---|---|
| [`xqffi`](xqffi/) | PyO3 FFI bindings for `xqvm` + `xqasm` (`xqffi.vm`, `xqffi.asm`, `xqffi.verifier`) |
| [`xqvm_py`](xqvm_py/) | Pure-Python reference VM (conformance oracle) |
| [`xqcp`](xqcp/) | Constraint-programming DSL that compiles to `.xqasm` |
| [`xqsa`](xqsa/) | Solver adapters -- CPU/GPU annealers, D-Wave QPU, Quip network |
| [`xquad`](xquad/) | Umbrella meta-package with interactive `Program` / `Session` / `RunResult` API, and the `xquad` CLI (`xquad vm asm` / `dis` / `run` / `check`) |

The one Rust package without a crates.io artefact is the `xqffi` pyo3
crate itself -- it ships as the `xqffi` PyPI wheel rather than a reusable
Rust library.

## Quick start

### A minimal program (CLI)

```asm
; add.xqasm -- push two integers and add them
PUSH 10
PUSH 32
ADD
HALT
```

```sh
xquad vm asm add.xqasm -o add.xqb && xquad vm run add.xqb
```

### End-to-end (Python, via the umbrella)

The recommended user-facing surface is `xquad.program.Program` +
`Session` + `RunResult`. Load once, run many times with different
calldata, inspect outputs by slot:

```python
from xquad.program import Program

program = Program.from_source("""
PUSH 0
INPUT r0
PUSH 1
INPUT r1
LOAD r0
LOAD r1
ADD
STOW r2
PUSH 0
OUTPUT r2
HALT
""")

session = program.session(output_slots=1)
session.set_calldata([40, 2])
result = session.run()
assert dict(result.outputs) == {0: 42}
```

`Program.load(bytes)` takes wire-format bytecode; `Session.run()`
returns a `RunResult` with dict-keyed outputs (unset slots present as
`None`), residual stack, and step count. See
[Running Programs](docs/book/src/running/README.md) for the full tour.

#### Low-level / conformance surface

For conformance harnesses and one-shot execution, the raw
`xqffi.vm.Vm` is still available directly:

```python
from xqffi.asm import assemble_source
from xqffi.vm import Vm

bytecode = assemble_source(src)
v = Vm()
v.set_calldata([40, 2])
v.set_output_slots(1)
v.run(bytecode)
assert v.outputs() == [42]
```

The `xquad.vm.VM` class offers a middle tier -- a unified wrapper with
backend dispatch (`VMBackend.RUST` / `VMBackend.PYTHON`) that accepts
`.xqasm` source and normalises types across the two interpreters.

### End-to-end worked example

[`examples/tsp/`](examples/tsp/) shows a full Travelling Salesman Problem
driven from the `xqcp` DSL through the VM and `xqsa` solver, runnable on
either the Python reference VM or the Rust VM:

```sh
uv run python examples/tsp/runner.py --seed 42
uv run python examples/maxcut/runner.py --seed 42 --interpreter rust

# Run every example on both interpreters, check each finds a valid solution:
make example-smoke
```

## Architecture

XQuad is a stack-based interpreter with a 256-slot register file. Registers
hold typed values -- integers, integer vectors, QUBO/Ising models
(`XqmxModel`), and candidate solutions (`XqmxSample`). A dedicated loop stack
drives `RANGE`/`ITER` iteration.

The opcode table is declared once in `xqvm/src/bytecode/types/table.rs` via
the `opcodes!` x-macro; `conformance/opcodes.yaml` is the machine-readable
mirror that all three representations (YAML, Rust macro, `xqvm_py.opcodes`)
are checked against at build time and in CI
(`scripts/check-opcode-parity.py`).

The binary format (`.xqb`) opens with a fixed 15-byte XQBC header --
magic, version, calldata/output-slot counts, code length, and a CRC-32
checksum of the payload -- followed by the instruction stream: an
opcode byte followed by its operands in big-endian byte order.

See [`conformance/opcodes.md`](conformance/opcodes.md) for
instruction-by-instruction semantics and
[`spec/xqvm/SPEC.md`](spec/xqvm/SPEC.md) for the normative spec.

## Development

### Prerequisites

```sh
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh   # stable Rust
make deps                                                          # dev tools
```

### Local setup

```sh
make xquad
```

This syncs the Python workspace (`xqvm_py`, `xqcp`, `xqsa`, `xqffi`,
`xquad`) into `.venv/`, builds the `xqffi` pyo3 extension via maturin,
puts the repo root on `sys.path` so scripts anywhere in the repo can
`import xqcp` / `xqsa` / `xqvm_py` / `xqffi` / `xquad` naturally, and
installs the `xquad` command into `.venv/bin/`, run with `uv run xquad`.

Open a REPL with everything ready:

```sh
make repl
```

### CI-equivalent locally

```sh
make preflight    # what CI enforces, split into preflight-rs / -py / -parity / -docs / -policy
make conformance  # cross-impl parity suite (Rust + Python)
```

### Contributing

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for the development workflow, commit
conventions, and DCO sign-off requirements. Agent guidelines for AI coding
assistants are in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md); cutting a release is documented in
[RELEASING.md](RELEASING.md).

`pip install xquad` now installs the `xquad` command, with the XQVM tools under `xquad vm` and a new `xquad quip` group for Quip accounts, job orders and receipts. SolverQuip gains named accounts, a read-only client and a TLS context option, and every job order it sends now settles from finalized chain state. SolverQuip needs a Quip network on runtime 119 or later.

### Highlights

- The `xquad` CLI ships with `pip install xquad` (or `python -m xquad`): `xquad vm asm`, `dis`, `run` and `check`, with the flags, output and exit codes of `xqcli`.
- `xquad quip account list|show|new|import|use` manages named Quip accounts at project and user level; `xquad quip orders`, `status` and `reclaim` read and reclaim an account's job orders. `--json` gives machine-readable output.
- SolverQuip resolves its signer through named Quip accounts, and `SolverQuip(read_only=True)` reads balances, orders and receipts without loading a key. New `balance()`, `reserved()` and `order_slots()`.
- `SolverQuip(ssl_context=...)` uses your TLS context for the RPC connection and the faucet request, for example to check revocation.
- `xqffi.vm.Vm.run` writes the VM's text or JSON trace to a file.

releases.name: v0.4.4
releases.body:
`SolverQuip` now shows what an order paid, both on a submitted order and on a failed one, and names accounts in SS58 form in its warnings, prompts and errors. A raw access dict that cannot be read is refused when the option is checked, instead of failing later. The book and spec drop the runtime 119 caveats.

### Highlights

- A submitted order's box shows the fee it paid, and a failed order shows the fee it was charged.
- The unregistered-solver warning, the autofund prompt, balance errors and faucet errors name accounts in SS58 form. Display falls back to hex when the chain's SS58 format is unknown.
- An unreadable raw access dict raises `QuipOrderOptionError("access")`: at construction for a client default, per order otherwise.
- The book notes that SolverQuip's TLS clients do not check certificate revocation, and how to fail closed.

### Behaviour changes

- Messages that named an account in hex now use SS58. Code that parses these messages needs updating.
- The refusal to reclaim an answered order now reads "awaits a claim" rather than "awaits the winner's claim".

releases.name: v0.4.3
releases.body:
Job orders on the Quip Network. `SolverQuip.create_order` places an order you can follow, read back through its receipt, and reclaim. Orders take payout rules, access rules and quality floors. Coefficients are now rounded to milli precision instead of refused, and the Quip modules move into the `xqsa.quip` package; the old names still work until v0.5.0.

### Highlights

- `SolverQuip.create_order(model)` returns a `JobOrder`. `list_orders()` and `get_receipt(id)` read orders back, `JobOrder.best()` and `JobOrder.solutions()` decode the answers, and a receipt can reclaim its order.
- Payout rules: `ResolutionSingleBest`, `ResolutionTopNEqual(n)` and `ResolutionTopNWeighted(n)`. Top-N orders settle on the receipt.
- Access rules: `AccessOpen()` and `AccessAllow(accounts=…, types=…)` restrict which solvers may answer.
- Quality floors: `max_energy`, `min_solutions` and `min_diversity`.
- Orders, quotes and receipts print as readable boxes.

releases.name: v0.4.2
releases.body:
The `xquad` Python backend now applies the same size, grid and index checks as the Rust backend, so a program is refused the same way whichever backend runs it. `xqffi` refuses model state no program could build, and the VM reads bytecode faster.

### Highlights

- Both `xquad` backends refuse the same calldata, at `set_calldata` and at run time. Sample entries past the model size, which the Rust backend used to drop, are refused too.
- `xqffi` model and sample constructors check their grid and size up front.
- Faster bytecode reads in the VM and the verifier, with no change to semantics or step metering.
- `xqvm::grid_fits` and `xqffi.vm.MAX_ALLOCATION_SIZE` are public.

### Behaviour changes

- `XqmxModel` and `XqmxSample` raise `ValueError` when the grid is neither 0x0 nor fits the size, or when the size exceeds `MAX_ALLOCATION_SIZE`.
- `set_linear`, `get_linear`, `set_quad` and `get_quad` raise `IndexError` for an index at or past the size. The setters used to grow the model silently.
- A negative coefficient index raises `IndexError` instead of `OverflowError`.

releases.name: v0.4.1
releases.body:
`SolverQuip` can take a model to the Quip Network end to end: pick a network preset, quote the job, fund the account from a faucet, and submit. Funding and submission go through two consent gates, which proceed by default and can be set to ask first. The book adds a first Quip job tutorial.

### Highlights

- Network presets: `SolverQuip.for_network("aglais")` for Quip TestNet, and `"devnet"` for a local node.
- `SolverQuip.quote(model)` returns a `JobQuote` with the reward, the fee and the account balance before anything is proposed.
- A faucet client, `fund_from_faucet`, tops up an underfunded account.
- Consent gates: `autoconfirm` and `autofund` each take `True`, `False` (ask at the terminal) or a callable that receives the `JobQuote`. They are also set by `QUIP_AUTOCONFIRM` and `QUIP_AUTOFUND`.
- Native topology mode (`topology="native"`) submits a model over the network's own coupling graph.

### Behaviour changes

- With no seed or keystore given, `SolverQuip` creates or reuses `~/.quip/keystore.json` and logs a warning. It used to raise `ValueError`. Pass `seed=` or `keystore=` to choose the account.
- `autofund` defaults to `True`: an underfunded `solve()` draws one faucet

aiSummary.oneLiner: A decentralized protocol enabling cross-chain quadratic funding and verifiable credential voting for Web3.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: XQuad functions as a universal intermediate representation and toolchain for quadratic optimization problems, bridging the gap between quantum annealers and classical solvers. It provides a highly specified virtual machine architecture, akin to LLVM for quadratic models, allowing developers to write an optimization problem once and target any supported backend. The project includes a robust Rust core designed to be embeddable in constrained environments, alongside Python distributions for broader accessibility. By enforcing strict parity between the Rust production VM and the Python reference VM, it ensures absolute reliability across diverse hardware targets.
keyFeatures: Hardware-agnostic compilation: Translates quadratic optimization problems into a common intermediate representation suitable for varied hardware targets.
Strict specification enforcement: Ensures absolute behavioral parity between the Rust production VM and Python reference VM via continuous integration.
Embeddable Rust core: Designed with no_std support, allowing the virtual machine to be deployed in highly constrained environments.
Multi-language ecosystem: Ships as an integrated suite of Rust crates and Python distributions to support a wide range of scientific developers.
Quantum and classical backend support: Allows execution on both cutting-edge quantum annealers and traditional classical compute solvers.

useCases.title: Algorithm development
useCases.description: Researchers develop and test complex quadratic optimization algorithms in Python before compiling them for high-performance quantum hardware.

useCases.title: Hardware benchmarking
useCases.description: Data scientists use the common intermediate representation to run the exact same optimization problem across classical and quantum solvers for performance comparison.

useCases.title: Embedded optimization
useCases.description: Engineers deploy the lightweight Rust core into edge devices to perform local optimization tasks without relying on external cloud compute.

useCases.title: Cross-platform research
useCases.description: Academic teams utilize the toolchain to guarantee their optimization models behave identically regardless of the underlying execution environment.

aiSummary.whoIsItFor: Quantum computing researchers, data scientists, and systems engineers working on advanced optimization problems across diverse hardware platforms. Familiarity with constraint-programming workflows is highly recommended for optimal usage.
aiSummary.gettingStarted: Review the specification in spec/xqvm/SPEC.md and explore the Rust crates or Python distributions.
